work.title: When You Help Others, You're Asking Them to Hold Your Fear
work.speaker: Joe Hudson
work.gem: Constantly helping people who haven't asked is usually driven by the helper's own fear. It disempowers the people being helped and leaves both sides resentful. The way out is to carry that fear yourself, help only when asked, and ask plainly for what you need.
work.cliff: People who help all the time, at work, in a marriage, as parents, often end up resentful and unsupported, while the people they help feel doubted and start to resent them back. Help nobody asked for tells people they can't manage on their own, and it hands them the helper's anxiety to carry. The person being helped plays a part too, accepting the helping as a stand-in for the care they really want. The habit most likely goes back to a childhood spent looking after a parent's feelings. Getting out of it means apologising, agreeing to help only when asked, owning the fear instead of passing it on, asking people what they actually want, and, for anyone who leads, asking for just enough information to feel safe.
summary: People who constantly help others often find themselves resentful and unable to get the help they need themselves. The talk is written from experience: the speaker was that kind of person for a very long time.

A man in a position of authority, always stepping in for the people he oversees, shows how it works. The first effect is that it typically [[distrust|disempowers the people being helped]]. Help that wasn't asked for is like taking on someone's credit card debt without paying it off: the debt is not relieved, only doubled. It tells them they can't do it alone and aren't trusted, and it makes them feel less about themselves. Help that someone asks for is very different.

Help like this typically [[fear|comes from fear of getting in trouble]]: that someone will be upset, or something will go wrong. Acting on it hands the anxiety to someone else to hold. The same man was building a house; things went badly, his whole vacation was swallowed by stress, and he came back to work depleted. His wife is an architect, and she had not asked for his help. Seeing that opened a simpler arrangement: she could ask if she needed him.

The pattern turns up all the time in marriages and companies. A boss helps everyone, then wonders why they are doing everything alone, when they could hold clear expectations and ask people to say if they can't manage or need help. Parents help a teenager with everything and get a teenager who is despondent, angry and resentful, which is what happens when people are treated as incapable. Underneath, the helper is asking: will you hold my fear? This is the helper trap.

Those on the receiving end, watching this and feeling above it, are [[surrogate|part of the pattern too]]. They take the helping as a stand-in for the care they really want, giving up their own truth for something close to care. They feel loved and undermined at once, and don't stand up for themselves. It is not a one-way street.

The way out begins with [[own|an apology, an agreement, and owning the fear]]: telling the people involved you are sorry for disempowering them and will stop stepping in unless they ask. When fear of a consequence rises, it is owned, not acted on, and not even voiced, because voicing it hands it over too. They are invited to say "relax" when they see it happening.

The helper mindset [[origin|most likely begins in childhood]], in a relationship where the child's job was to look after the parents' feelings rather than the other way round, and not doing so brought trouble. So the adult keeps helping to stay out of trouble, whether the feeling is guilt or something more frightening. Owning that openly with people matters too.

Most people don't want help given out of obligation, any more than they would want to come to a party they were invited to only out of obligation. If someone does want that, the relationship deserves a closer look, with compassion. [[want|Naming the guilt and asking what they actually want]], how they would like to be helped and what it would be like for them simply to ask, is a very quick way to change the pattern.

Anyone who leads has one more step. Since people working without reporting would create a lot of anxiety, [[leader|agree on the minimum information needed to feel safe]]. The same may hold for parents. There may be pushback at first, until people see it means the helping will stop.

Finally, [[ask|make sure your own needs are met]]. The real shift is from taking care of yourself by taking care of others to taking care of yourself directly, which means knowing what you need and asking for it.

concepts.name: Unasked help disempowers
concepts.gem: Help that nobody asked for carries a quiet message: you can't do this on your own. Instead of lightening someone's load, it adds the weight of being doubted.
concepts.cliff: It is like taking on someone's credit card debt without paying it off: the debt is not relieved, only doubled. The person still has the work, and now also the feeling of not being trusted with it. Over time that erodes trust and makes them feel smaller. Help that is asked for is a different thing entirely.
full: Constant helping, let me do this for you, let me do that, typically disempowers the very people it is meant to serve. Without saying so, unasked help tells them: you can't do it on your own, I don't believe in you, I don't trust you to get it done. It takes on their work without taking it away from them.

Credit card debt is the image for it. Taking on someone's debt without relieving it simply doubles it: they keep the burden and gain the sense of being doubted. Trust erodes, and they come to feel less about themselves.

At full scale it looks like this. Parents who help a teenager with everything, remembering, cleaning the room, grades, getting into college, end up with a teenager who is despondent, angry and resentful. That is what happens when people are treated as incapable. A boss caught in the same pattern ends up wondering why they are doing everything alone. The alternative is to hold clear expectations: this is what I expect; tell me if you can't do it, if you need help, if you need advice. Then people feel trusted to get the job done.

quotes.text: if you're helping somebody without them asking for help, you're basically taking on their credit card debt, but you're not relieving them of it. You're just doubling the credit card debt.
I'm telling you you can't do it on your own. I'm telling you that I don't believe in you.
That's what happens when you treat people like they're incapable.

concepts.name: Helping hands them your fear
concepts.gem: Much unasked help comes from fear: that someone will be upset, that something will go wrong, that there will be trouble. Acting on that fear passes the anxiety to the person being helped, who ends up holding it for the helper.
concepts.cliff: A man who oversaw other people was building a house. When things went badly he spent his whole vacation stressed, helping his wife, and came back to work depleted. She is an architect, and had not asked for help. The question that changed it was whether she had asked at all, or whether he had simply stressed out and left her feeling disempowered. Underneath, the helper is asking: will you hold my fear?
full: When help is given to people who haven't asked, it is typically because the helper is scared of getting in trouble: someone will get upset, or something will go wrong without them. The helping takes all that anxiety and hands it to someone else to hold. In incessant helping this happens again and again.

The house is a clear case. Very bad things went wrong, the man was completely stressed, his vacation was ruined, and he arrived at work depleted. Asked whether his wife even wanted the help, given that she is an architect, he had the look of someone realising he might be doing something different from what he thought. From there a simpler arrangement became possible: she could ask for help if she needed it, and then he could get involved instead of stepping in and disempowering her.
Put in one line, constant helping says: will you hold my fear? I'm scared, and I don't trust you to actually do your work.

quotes.text: if you're helping somebody like that, it's because you're scared to get in trouble.
What you're doing is you're taking all that anxiety, you're just handing it to someone else to hold for you.
It's because what you're actually doing is you're saying, "Hey, will you hold my fear? Hey, I'm scared and I don't trust you to actually do your work."

concepts.name: The person being helped is part of it
concepts.gem: The person on the receiving end of constant help is part of the pattern too. The helping can stand in for the care they really want, so they settle for being undermined instead of asking for that care.
concepts.cliff: It is easy to watch a helper and feel above it. But the helping offers something close to care, and that closeness is hard to give up. So instead of saying what care is actually wanted, the person helped gives up their own truth, feels loved and undermined at once, and doesn't stand up for themselves. The pattern runs both ways.
full: Anyone who hears about the helper trap and thinks of the helper in their own life, with a certain smugness, is absolutely part of the pattern as well.

Their part is that the helping supplies a surrogate of care. Rather than asking for the care they really want, rather than saying they won't hold the helper's fear, or that they can get the job done if treated a particular way, they sacrifice their own truth for some close proximity to care.
The result is a mixed feeling: this person loves me, and this person undermines me. And they are not standing up for themselves. It is not a one-way street.

quotes.text: the way that you're a part of that pattern is that you're getting a surrogate of care with this helping. Instead of asking for the care that you really want
you're sacrificing what your truth is for some close proximity to care.
So, it's it's not a one-way street.

concepts.name: Apologise, agree, and own the fear
concepts.gem: The way out starts with an apology and an agreement: no more stepping in unless asked. When fear of a consequence rises, it is owned rather than acted on, and not even voiced, because voicing it hands it over too.
concepts.cliff: The apology names what has been happening: sorry for disempowering you by coming to your aid when you didn't ask. The agreement is that help now waits to be asked for. The fear behind the urge to control is noticed and kept, not passed on. And the other person is invited to say "relax, you don't need to do this" whenever the old habit shows.
full: The first step is to look at the people involved and tell them: I realise, and I'm sorry, that I've been disempowering you by constantly coming to your aid without you asking, and I'm going to stop unless you ask me.

When there is fear of a consequence, it is owned: I notice I want to control things because I'm scared right now. Even naming what the fear is about would hand it to the other person, so it is held without being handed to anybody.

Then a clear agreement is made, with colleagues, family or a partner: unless you ask, I won't step in and try to help. If you see me doing it, just tell me to relax, that I don't need to do this right now. They might even say: you're not going to get in trouble if you don't help me; I actually want to do this on my own.

quotes.text: I realize and I'm sorry for disempowering you by constantly coming to your aid without you asking. And I'm going to stop doing that unless you ask me.
I'm not going to even tell you what I'm scared about because then I'll be handing it off to you.
So, there's just an owning the fear without actually handing it to somebody.

concepts.name: Where the urge to help begins
concepts.gem: The urge to keep helping most likely began in childhood, in a family where the child's job was to look after the parents' feelings rather than the other way round, and where not helping brought trouble.
concepts.cliff: A child in that position learns that helping keeps them safe. The adult carries the lesson on, helping to stay out of trouble. The felt consequence might be guilt, or something as frightening as being hit, but there is always a sense that not helping will bring trouble. Saying this openly to the people involved is part of changing it.
full: There is something strange about the helper mindset. What has most likely happened is a reversed relationship with one's parents: the child's job was to help the parents emotionally, rather than the parents' job being to help the child. When the child didn't, there was trouble.

So the grown helper is constantly trying to avoid trouble by helping people. That is what is actually going on. It might show up as guilt when not helping, or as a fear of being hit. Whatever the form, there is a consequence that feels real: if I don't help them, I'll be in trouble.
Owning this with people is important too, said simply: I feel guilty when I'm not helping you.

quotes.text: what has happened to you most likely is that you were in a relationship with your parents where your job was to help them emotionally rather than their job was helping you emotionally.
you're constantly just trying to avoid trouble by helping people. That's what's actually going on.

concepts.name: Name the guilt, ask what they want
concepts.gem: Help given out of guilt or obligation is rarely wanted, any more than an invitation given only out of obligation. Naming the guilt and asking how the other person actually wants to be helped changes the pattern quickly.
concepts.cliff: Hearing "I'm only helping because I feel obligated" would put most people off the help entirely. So the honest move is to say it: I feel guilty, I feel obligated, and I don't want to act from that; what do you want? Most people turn out not to want the guilt at all. If someone does want help given from obligation, that relationship deserves a closer look, with compassion.
full: One way to open it: I feel guilty when I'm not helping you. How do you feel about that? Do you want me to feel guilty when I'm not helping you? Most people, asked this, find they don't, and they certainly don't want action taken out of obligation.

If someone said they were helping only because they felt obligated, the help would probably not be wanted. If someone said the party invitation came only from obligation, the party would probably not be attended. And if a person really does want help given that way, the relationship is worth questioning a little. It may be a pattern they are used to, so there is compassion to be had.

The conversation itself: I don't want to act out of obligation or guilt, but I feel guilty and obligated. What do you want? How do you want me to help you? What would it be like for you to just ask me for help, so I know I'm actually being useful to you instead of undermining you? It is a very quick way to change the pattern, and with luck the other person will also say when the helping has started again and isn't needed.

quotes.text: if I was to say to you, "I'm helping you cuz I feel obligated," you would probably not want my help.
I don't want to act out of obligation. I don't want to act out of guilt. But I feel guilty. I feel obligated. What do you want?
It's a really great very quick way to change the pattern.

concepts.name: For leaders: just enough information
concepts.gem: Leading people without hovering over them needs one thing in place: an agreed, minimal flow of information, just enough to feel safe about how the work is going.
concepts.cliff: Once the helping stops, people may simply go off, do the work, and report only that it's done or not done. For someone responsible for the result, that would create a great deal of anxiety. So the minimum needed to feel safe is agreed in advance, perhaps a two-minute report. Parents face the same need. People may resist at first, until they see it means the hovering is over.
full: Leadership adds a complication. Once the helping stops, people will often want to go and do the thing without saying anything, and then simply announce it is done, or not done. A leader can't work that way; it would create too much anxiety.

The answer is to find the minimal amount of information needed to feel safe about how things are going. The same may hold for parents, who carry responsibility for a child being happy and learning, as a leader carries responsibility for an organisation being happy and healthy. Some information is genuinely needed.
There may be pushback at first. Then people realise it means no more being helped all the time, and the response changes: this is great, I'll happily write the two-minute report.

quotes.text: So you have to find a way that you can get the minimal amount of information you need so that you can feel safe about how it's going.
Then they're going to be like, "This is great. Yeah, I'll I'll write the 2-minute report. Happy to do it."

concepts.name: Taking care of yourself by asking
concepts.gem: The deepest shift is from taking care of yourself by taking care of others to taking care of yourself directly. That means knowing what you need and asking for it.
concepts.cliff: Constant helping was a roundabout way of meeting one's own needs. When it stops, those needs still have to be met, and the only direct way is to ask. Being clear about what is needed is what finally allows the constant, almost compulsive helping to let go.
full: Alongside everything else, one's own needs have to be met. The move is from taking care of yourself by taking care of others, to taking care of yourself by taking care of yourself, which means asking for things.
That is why clarity matters so much. Knowing what you need is what lets go of constantly, maniacally, automatically helping people.

quotes.text: just make sure that your needs are met at the same time because you're going from taking care of yourself by taking care of others into taking care of yourself by taking care of yourself, which means asking for stuff.
it's really important that you're clear on what you need so that you can let go of constantly, maniacally, automatically helping people.
